question: In Java 17, when does an object become eligible for garbage collection?
options: As soon as one of its reference variables is set to null
When no GC root can reach it through a chain of strong references
After its finalize method has been called once
After it has gone unused for a time limit chosen by the JVM
explanation: Garbage collection in HotSpot is based on reachability. An object is eligible when no GC root (thread stack, static field, and so on) can reach it through strong references. Setting one variable to null only removes one path, and other references may still keep the object alive. Unused time and finalization are not the criteria.

question: Which of the following is a GC root?
options: Any object stored in the young generation
Any object whose class overrides equals
Any object that has survived at least one collection
A local variable holding a reference on an active thread's stack
explanation: GC roots are starting points of the reachability trace: local variables and operands on active thread stacks, static fields of loaded classes, JNI references, and similar. Where an object lives (young or old generation) or how many collections it survived does not make it a root.

question: Assume Java 17. After the three null assignments in main, how many of the three Node objects are still strongly reachable from a GC root?
explanation: After the assignments no local variable refers to any node. The objects a and b reference each other, forming an island of isolation, and c references a, but nothing outside the group points in. Tracing from the roots reaches none of them, so all three are unreachable. References between garbage objects do not keep them alive.

question: How does the HotSpot JVM decide that an object is garbage?
options: It counts references to each object and frees the object when the count reaches zero
It counts references and runs a background thread that breaks reference cycles
It traces from GC roots and treats every object it cannot reach as garbage, even if those objects reference each other
It relies on compiler-inserted free calls at the end of each block
explanation: HotSpot collectors are tracing collectors: they mark everything reachable from the roots and treat the rest as garbage. This is why cyclic structures that nothing reaches are still collected, which pure reference counting cannot do.

question: What happens when this program is compiled?
options: It compiles and prints x0x1x1
Compile-time error: sb is out of scope at the last println
It compiles and throws NullPointerException at run time
It compiles and prints x0x1null
explanation: A variable declared inside the loop body exists only within that block. Using it after the loop is a compile-time 'cannot find symbol' error. Scope is a compile-time visibility rule and is separate from object lifetime, which the garbage collector decides by reachability.

question: Which statement best summarizes the relationship between variable scope and an object's eligibility for garbage collection?
options: Leaving a variable's scope only removes one reference; the object is collectable only when no strong path from any root remains
Leaving a variable's scope immediately frees the object it referred to
An object becomes collectable as soon as the block that created it ends, whatever other references exist
Objects can be collected only after the whole method that created them has returned
explanation: Scope controls which names are visible, not how long objects live. An object stays alive while any strong reference chain from a root exists, for example through a field, a collection, or another live variable.

question: Which statement about System.gc() in Java 17 is correct?
options: It forces an immediate collection and guarantees that every unreachable object is reclaimed before it returns
It runs the finalizers of all objects without performing a collection
It is a compile-time directive that is ignored at run time
It is only a request; the JVM may ignore it, and -XX:+DisableExplicitGC makes HotSpot ignore it
explanation: The specification only says that calling System.gc() suggests the JVM spend effort reclaiming memory. HotSpot usually does run a collection by default, but there is no guarantee, and the flag -XX:+DisableExplicitGC turns the call into a no-op. Application logic must never depend on it.

question: Which list orders the java.lang.ref reachability strengths from strongest to weakest?
options: strong, weak, soft, phantom
strong, soft, weak, phantom
soft, strong, weak, phantom
strong, phantom, soft, weak
explanation: Strong references are the strongest, then soft references (cleared under memory pressure), then weak references (cleared once the referent is only weakly reachable), then phantom references (used for post-mortem cleanup). An object's reachability is that of its strongest path.

explanation: The local variable o is a strong reference that is still used in the comparison, so the object is strongly reachable and the weak reference cannot be cleared. A WeakReference is cleared only when its referent is no longer strongly or softly reachable.

The string form of the Object
true
It does not compile because PhantomReference has no get method
explanation: PhantomReference.get() always returns null, even while the referent is strongly reachable. A phantom reference exists only to be enqueued after the referent is finalized and ready for reclamation, so it cannot be used to retrieve the object.

question: Which reference type is designed for memory-sensitive caches, because HotSpot clears it only under memory pressure and always before throwing OutOfMemoryError?
options: WeakReference
PhantomReference
A strong reference stored in a HashMap
SoftReference
explanation: Soft references are retained as long as memory is plentiful and are cleared before the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError, which suits caches. Weak references are cleared at the next collection once weakly reachable, and phantom references cannot return their referent at all.

question: A WeakHashMap<Session, SessionData> is used, and each SessionData holds a strong field reference back to its own Session key. What is the consequence?
options: Entries disappear as soon as the application drops its last outside reference to the Session
The map throws IllegalStateException when a value references its key
Entries are never removed, because the value is strongly reachable from the map and keeps its key strongly reachable
Entries are removed only when the map grows past its load factor
explanation: WeakHashMap holds only its keys weakly; values are held strongly. If a value refers back to its key, the map's strong path to the value also reaches the key, so the key never becomes weakly reachable and the entry is never purged. This is a classic WeakHashMap trap.

question: Which statement about Object.finalize() in Java 17 is correct?
options: It is deprecated since Java 9, and the JVM gives no guarantee that it runs promptly or at all
It was removed from Object in Java 11, so overriding it no longer compiles
It is guaranteed to run before the object's memory is reclaimed
It is called automatically at the end of every method that allocated the object
explanation: finalize() is deprecated (since Java 9) because it is unpredictable, slow, and can resurrect objects. The JVM does not promise when, or even whether, it runs. It still exists in Java 17, so overriding it compiles with a deprecation warning.

question: Inside finalize(), an object stores this into a static field, making itself reachable again. What does the JVM guarantee about this object's future?
options: Its finalize() method is invoked again every time it later becomes unreachable
Its finalize() method will not be invoked again for that object, even if it later becomes unreachable
The JVM throws IllegalStateException when the resurrection occurs
It can never be garbage collected afterwards, even after the static reference is removed
explanation: The JVM runs finalize() at most once per object. A resurrected object can be collected normally later if it becomes unreachable again, but its finalizer is not run a second time. Resurrection is one of the reasons finalizers are discouraged.

question: Which approach is recommended in Java 17 for deterministically releasing a native resource such as a file handle?
options: Override finalize() and call System.gc() when finished
Rely on the JVM to close the resource when its object becomes unreachable
Set the reference to null and wait for the collector
Implement AutoCloseable and use try-with-resources, optionally backed by a Cleaner as a safety net
explanation: Garbage collection manages memory, not external resources, and its timing is unpredictable. try-with-resources closes the resource at a known point. A java.lang.ref.Cleaner can serve as a backup if a caller forgets to close, but it must not be the primary mechanism.

question: What is the output?

body close B close A end
close B close A body end
body end close B close A
explanation: The try body runs first. Resources are then closed in the reverse order of their declaration, so B is closed before A, and only after that does the code following the statement run.

question: Which situation is a typical logical memory leak in a Java application?
options: A local ArrayList that goes out of scope when its method returns
Creating many short-lived temporary strings inside a loop
A static Map used as a cache that is added to on every request but never evicted
Calling System.gc() inside a request handler
explanation: A Java memory leak means objects that are no longer needed are still strongly reachable. A static map is reachable from a class root for the whole program, so entries that are never removed accumulate. Short-lived locals and temporary strings become unreachable quickly.

question: Which statement completes pop() so the stack does not retain an obsolete reference to the removed element?
options: elements[size] = null;
elements[size] = result;
size = size - 1;
result = null;
explanation: After --size, the slot at index size still holds the popped element, so the backing array keeps it strongly reachable even though the stack no longer uses it. Clearing that slot removes the obsolete reference. Setting the local variable result to null does nothing useful because the array slot is the leaking path.

question: Why can values stored in a ThreadLocal leak when threads come from a thread pool?
options: ThreadLocal values are held in a static field of ThreadLocal, so they can never be collected
ThreadLocal values are copied to every thread in the pool permanently
Calling ThreadLocal.get() disables garbage collection for its thread
Pool threads are long-lived, and each thread's ThreadLocalMap keeps the value strongly reachable until remove() is called or the thread ends
explanation: The value lives in a map owned by the Thread object. A pooled thread survives across many tasks, so a value set during one task stays reachable unless the code calls remove(), typically in a finally block.

question: Short-lived screen objects register themselves as listeners on a long-lived event bus and never unregister. What is the effect?
options: The screens are collected normally because listeners are held through weak references by default
The bus's listener list keeps each screen strongly reachable, so they accumulate until they are unregistered
The JVM unregisters listeners automatically when the owning object's method returns
The screens are collected, but their callbacks keep running on freed memory
explanation: A long-lived object that holds strong references to registered listeners keeps them reachable. Unless the code unregisters them (or the bus uses weak references explicitly), they leak. The JVM never unregisters listeners on its own.

question: Which sequence correctly describes the lifecycle of a typical Java object?
options: Allocated, in use, finalized, unreachable, reclaimed
In use, allocated, unreachable, reclaimed
Created (allocated and initialized), in use, unreachable, then reclaimed by the collector
Created, in use, reclaimed by the programmer with delete, unreachable
explanation: An object is allocated and initialized by its constructor, used while reachable, becomes unreachable when the last strong path disappears, and its memory is then reclaimed by the garbage collector. Finalization, if any, happens only after the object has become unreachable, and Java has no delete operator.

explanation: Memory for the whole object is allocated and zeroed first, so x holds its default value 0. The Parent constructor runs before Child's field initializers, and the overridden show() is called virtually, so it prints x=0. Calling overridable methods from constructors exposes a half-initialized object.

question: In the Java memory model as implemented by HotSpot (ignoring JIT optimizations), where do the object created by new Foo() and the local variable foo that refers to it live?
options: The object is on the heap; the reference variable is in the current method's stack frame
Both are on the thread stack
The object is in Metaspace; the variable is on the heap
Both are on the heap
explanation: Objects are allocated on the garbage-collected heap, while local variables, including references, live in the stack frame of the executing method. The stack frame is what makes the heap object reachable. Metaspace holds class metadata, not instances.

question: After work() returns and before the println runs, which Box objects are still strongly reachable?
options: Neither Box, because work() has returned
Only the Box holding 1
Both Box objects, because they were created in the same method
Only the Box holding 2, through the static field keep
explanation: When work() returns, its stack frame disappears and the locals a and b stop being roots. The Box holding 2 was also stored in the static field keep, which is a root, so it stays reachable. The Box holding 1 has no remaining path and becomes eligible.

question: What is the output?

false
NullPointerException
Compile-time error
explanation: Setting x to null only changes that variable. The object is still referenced by y, so y is not null and the object remains strongly reachable. An object becomes eligible only when every path to it is gone.

question: After arr = null executes, how many of the three Item objects are no longer strongly reachable?
explanation: The array held all three items. With arr set to null the array itself becomes unreachable, and so do the items only it referenced. The first item is also referenced by the variable first, so it stays reachable, leaving two unreachable items.

question: Since Java 7 (including Java 17), where is the string pool stored, and what can happen to interned strings that are no longer referenced?
options: The pool is on the heap, and interned strings that become unreachable can be garbage collected
The pool is in PermGen, and interned strings are never collected
The pool is on the thread stack and is cleared each time a method returns
The pool is in native memory, and interned strings are collected only through finalization
explanation: From Java 7 the string pool lives in the ordinary heap. Pooled strings are subject to normal reachability rules, so a string that nothing references can be collected. PermGen was removed entirely in Java 8.

question: Under which condition can HotSpot unload a class?
options: When no instances of the class exist, regardless of which class loader defined it
When the class has no static fields
After its static initializer has completed once
When its defining class loader, the Class object, and all of its instances are unreachable
explanation: Classes are tied to their class loader. They can be unloaded only when the loader and its Class objects are unreachable and no instances remain. Classes loaded by the built-in application loader are effectively never unloaded, which is why undeployed web applications can leak class loaders.

question: In Java 17, where does HotSpot store class metadata?
options: In the permanent generation inside the Java heap
In the young generation
In Metaspace, which uses native memory
In the code cache only
explanation: Since Java 8 the permanent generation has been replaced by Metaspace, which allocates class metadata from native memory and can be capped with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize. Objects (instances) still live in the heap.

question: What does the JVM do when it cannot satisfy an allocation request even after performing garbage collection?
options: It pauses the allocating thread until memory becomes available
It throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError to the allocating thread
It silently returns null from the new expression
It terminates the whole JVM immediately without any exception
explanation: If the heap cannot supply the memory after collection, the JVM throws OutOfMemoryError (for example 'Java heap space'). The expression new never yields null. The error can be caught, but recovery is rarely safe.

question: What is the output?

Compile-time error because an Error cannot be thrown
explanation: OutOfMemoryError extends VirtualMachineError, which extends Error, not Exception. The first catch does not match, so the Throwable handler runs. Errors can be thrown and caught like any Throwable, so this compiles.

question: When is a WeakReference placed on the ReferenceQueue it was registered with?
options: Immediately when the WeakReference object is constructed
When the application calls System.gc()
When the WeakReference object itself becomes unreachable
After the collector determines the referent is weakly reachable and clears the reference
explanation: Registration only associates the queue. The reference is enqueued after the garbage collector clears it because the referent is no longer strongly or softly reachable. Code can poll the queue to learn which referents were reclaimed.

question: What is the output?
options: null true
null false
java.lang.ref.WeakReference true
No output because poll blocks until a collection occurs
explanation: The object is still strongly referenced by o, so the weak reference has not been cleared or enqueued. ReferenceQueue.poll() is non-blocking and returns null when nothing is queued. get() still returns the same object, so the comparison is true.

question: An object is referenced only through one SoftReference and one WeakReference, with no strong references. How is it classified?
options: Weakly reachable
Softly reachable
Phantom reachable
Strongly reachable
explanation: Reachability is determined by the strongest remaining path. With no strong reference, the soft path is the strongest, so the object is softly reachable. The weak reference will not be cleared until the soft path is also gone.

question: A cache of decoded images should survive until memory gets tight, while a canonicalizing lookup table should drop entries as soon as callers stop using the keys. Which pairing fits?
options: Cache with WeakReference values, lookup table with SoftReference values
Both with PhantomReference
Cache with SoftReference values, lookup table with WeakHashMap keys
Both with strong references and explicit System.gc() calls
explanation: Soft references persist until memory pressure, which suits caches. Weak keys, as in WeakHashMap, let entries vanish once the application no longer uses the key. Swapping the two would drop cache entries too early or keep lookup entries too long.

question: Why does an object with a non-trivial finalize() method usually take at least two collection cycles to be reclaimed after it becomes unreachable?
options: Because finalize() can run only while the JVM performs a full collection of the old generation
Because the collector must wait until the young generation is completely full before it examines the object
Because the JVM first copies every finalizable object into Metaspace and then moves it back to the heap
Because it is first queued for finalization, and its memory is reclaimed only after the finalizer has run and a later cycle finds it still unreachable
explanation: A finalizable object must stay alive until its finalizer has run, since finalize() may use the object. Only a later collection that finds it unreachable again can free it. This delay is one reason finalizers hurt memory behavior.

question: Which implementation builds a comma-separated string of n numbers without creating a new intermediate String object on every iteration?
options: StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { sb.append(i).append(','); }
String s = ""; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { s += i + ","; }
String s = ""; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { s = s.concat(String.valueOf(i)).concat(","); }
String s = ""; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { s = String.format("%s%d,", s, i); }
explanation: StringBuilder appends into one growing buffer. Because String is immutable, each of the other versions allocates new String objects on every iteration, and the old ones become short-lived garbage. The total copying also grows quadratically.

question: The program prints 499500. What is the main allocation problem in this loop?
options: A String is created from sum on every iteration
The loop variable i is allocated on the heap each time
Each sum += i unboxes the value and boxes a new Long object once values exceed the Long cache range
The println call retains every previous value of sum
explanation: sum is a Long object, so every += unboxes, adds, and boxes the result into a new Long. Only values from -128 to 127 are cached, so beyond that each iteration creates garbage. Using the primitive long avoids it.

question: Which statement about escape analysis in the HotSpot JIT compiler is correct?
options: It moves every object to the old generation to avoid collections
It can let the JIT avoid heap allocation for objects that do not escape the method, for example by scalar replacement
It makes unreachable objects be collected before the method returns, as the Java language guarantees
It is a language rule that restricts which objects may be passed between threads
explanation: Escape analysis is an optimization, not a language rule. If the JIT proves an object never escapes a method or thread, it may eliminate the allocation by keeping the fields in registers or on the stack. This is why the 'every object is on the heap' model is only conceptual.

question: In a heap-dump analysis tool, what does the retained size of an object represent?
options: The size of the object's own fields only
The size of the object header in bytes
The total size of all objects reachable from it, even if they are shared with other roots
The memory that would be freed if the object were garbage collected, including objects reachable only through it
explanation: Retained size counts the object plus everything that would become unreachable if this object disappeared. Objects also reachable by other paths are excluded. Shallow size is only the object's own memory, so retained size is the number that matters when hunting leaks.

question: Assume Java 17 on Linux. Which command starts app.jar so that the JVM writes a heap dump automatically when an OutOfMemoryError occurs?
options: java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp -jar app.jar
java -XX:+PrintHeapAtGC -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp -jar app.jar
java -Xdump:oom=/tmp -jar app.jar
java -XX:+DisableExplicitGC -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp -jar app.jar
explanation: -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError enables the automatic dump, and -XX:HeapDumpPath chooses where it is written. HeapDumpPath alone has no effect without the first flag, and -Xdump belongs to a different JVM implementation.

question: Assume a JVM process with PID 4321 on Linux. Which command prints a histogram of live object counts per class, forcing a full collection first?
options: jstat -gc 4321
jinfo -flags 4321
jmap -histo:live 4321
jps -lv 4321
explanation: jmap -histo:live lists instance counts and sizes per class and counts only live objects, which makes the JVM run a full collection first. jstat reports GC statistics, jinfo shows flags, and jps lists JVM processes.

question: After outer = null, while inner remains in use, what is true of the InnerHold instance?
options: It is eligible for collection, because outer is null
It is eligible for collection, because Inner is a separate class
It becomes eligible after the next System.gc() call
It remains strongly reachable through the implicit reference held by the Inner instance
explanation: A non-static inner class instance holds a hidden reference to its enclosing instance. As long as inner is reachable, so is the InnerHold object and its 1 MB array. Declaring Inner as static removes the hidden reference.

question: Which JVM option sets the maximum Java heap size to 512 MB?
options: -Xmx512m
-Xms512m
-Xss512m
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m
explanation: -Xmx sets the maximum heap size. -Xms sets the initial heap, -Xss sets thread stack size, and -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize caps class metadata, not the object heap.

question: Which error message indicates that class metadata space is exhausted in Java 17?
options: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
java.lang.StackOverflowError
explanation: Metaspace replaced PermGen in Java 8, so exhausting it produces OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. 'Java heap space' refers to object memory and StackOverflowError to deep recursion on a thread stack.

question: What is the output?
options: cleaned twice, then end true
cleaned once, then end true
end true only, because cleaning happens only after a collection
cleaned once, then an IllegalStateException from the second clean call
explanation: Cleanable.clean() runs the registered action at most once, and calling it again does nothing. The first call runs the action synchronously on the calling thread, so cleaned prints before end. The cleaning action must not reference the owner object, otherwise it would never become unreachable.

question: Which expression correctly retrieves the referent, or null if it has been cleared?
options: ref.get()
ref.getReferent()
ref.value()
ref.deref()
explanation: java.lang.ref.Reference exposes get(), which returns the referent or null if it was cleared. Copying the result into a local strong variable and null-checking it is the safe pattern, because the object cannot disappear while the local reference exists.

question: A cache is a HashMap<String, SoftReference<byte[]>>. After the collector clears some soft references, what remains a problem, and how is it typically solved?
options: The map throws ConcurrentModificationException; the fix is to add synchronized blocks
The cleared values are replaced by empty arrays automatically, so nothing is needed
The stale keys are removed from the map automatically, so nothing is needed
The map still holds entries whose references are cleared; register a ReferenceQueue and purge stale entries
explanation: Clearing a SoftReference empties the reference object, but the HashMap still holds the key and the now-empty SoftReference, which is a small leak. Registering references with a ReferenceQueue lets the cache learn which ones were cleared and remove their entries.

question: Which statement about assigning null to local variables is the best practice?
options: Always set every local variable to null at the end of each method
Always set locals to null before calling System.gc()
It is usually unnecessary; it matters mainly when a long-lived object, such as a hand-managed array or field, would otherwise hold an obsolete reference
It is required before an object can be eligible for collection
explanation: Locals go away when the method returns, and the JIT already treats dead locals as unreachable, so nulling them adds noise. Nulling matters for long-lived holders, such as a stack's backing array, a field, or a cache, that would keep the object reachable.

question: Assume a default thread stack size on Java 17. What is the output?
options: The program hangs without output because the recursion never ends
SO
java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space is thrown
Compile-time error because f() has no base case
explanation: Each call adds a frame to the thread stack, not to the heap, so the stack is exhausted and the JVM throws StackOverflowError. The program does compile, and the error can be caught, so SO is printed. The garbage collector cannot reclaim active stack frames.

question: Pseudocode convention: every object has a reference count. Assigning to a variable increments the count of the new target object and decrements the count of the variable's previous target. An object is freed when its count reaches 0. Which objects have been freed after the last statement?
code:
A = new Obj1()
B = A
A = new Obj2()
B = null
options: Only Obj1
Only Obj2
Both Obj1 and Obj2
Neither Obj1 nor Obj2
explanation: Obj1 reaches count 2 after B = A, drops to 1 when A is reassigned, and drops to 0 when B becomes null, so it is freed. Obj2 still has count 1 through A. This is how reference counting works; the JVM instead traces from roots, which also handles cycles.

question: After the mark phase described in the pseudocode, how many of the objects R, A, B, C, and D are unmarked (garbage)?
code:
roots = { R }
edges:
    R -> A
    A -> B
    B -> A
    C -> B
    D -> C

mark = {}
visit(R)

visit(x):
    if x not in mark then
        add x to mark
        for every y such that x -> y
            visit(y)
explanation: Starting from R the trace marks R, A, and B (the A and B cycle is visited only once). C and D point into the marked region, but nothing reachable points to them, so they stay unmarked. Edges pointing into live objects do not make the source live; only edges out of reachable objects count.

question: In this pseudocode, mod is the remainder operator, and the variables obj and list are still in scope after the loop. After the loop ends, how many of the five Obj objects are strongly reachable?
code:
list = empty list
for i from 1 to 5:
    obj = new Obj(i)
    if i mod 2 == 0 then
        list.add(obj)
    end if
end for
explanation: The objects for i = 2 and i = 4 are stored in list. The variable obj still refers to the last object created, i = 5, so that one is reachable too. The objects for i = 1 and i = 3 were overwritten in obj and never stored, giving three reachable objects.

Compile-time error
explanation: Both a and b referred to the same ArrayList. Nulling a does not affect the list or its element, which remain reachable through b, so size() returns 1. Reachability is about paths, not about a particular variable.

question: The program prints ab. After s = s + "b" executes, which statement about the String literal "a" is correct?
options: It remains strongly reachable through the loaded class's constant pool, so it is not collectable while the class is loaded
It is immediately eligible because no variable refers to it
It is eligible only after the next young collection
It is copied into the new String, so the original is freed by the concatenation
explanation: String literals are interned and referenced from the class's constant pool. The variable s no longer refers to the literal, but the class does, so the literal stays reachable as long as the class is loaded. Concatenation creates a new String and does not free the old one.

question: A pooled worker thread is blocked forever waiting on a queue, and a local variable in its stack frame refers to a large byte array. What does this mean for the array?
options: The array is eligible, because a blocked thread is not running
The array is eligible, because blocked threads are not GC roots
The array is moved to the old generation and freed after the thread next wakes up
The array stays strongly reachable, because the stack frames of a live thread are GC roots
explanation: Thread stack locals are GC roots as long as the thread is alive, whether it is running or blocked. The array therefore stays reachable until the frame is popped or the variable is cleared. This is a common cause of leaks in long-lived pool threads.

question: Which class completes the declaration so that an entry disappears once its key is no longer strongly reachable elsewhere?
options: IdentityHashMap
LinkedHashMap
WeakHashMap
ConcurrentHashMap
explanation: Only WeakHashMap holds its keys through weak references, so an entry is removed after its key becomes weakly reachable. The other maps hold keys strongly and would keep every key alive, causing the entries to accumulate.

question: What is the output?
options: Compile-time error because this cannot be passed from a constructor
explanation: The constructor stores this in a static list, so the object is strongly reachable even though main ignores the result of new Escape(). Passing this from a constructor is legal, though it lets a partly constructed object escape, which is a known hazard.

question: Which observation motivates generational garbage collection in HotSpot?
options: Old objects are always larger than young objects
An object that survives one collection is guaranteed to die at the next one
Most objects die young, and the objects that survive tend to live for a long time
The lifetime of an object is proportional to its size
explanation: This is the weak generational hypothesis. Because most objects die soon after allocation, collecting a small young area often is cheap and reclaims most garbage, while the long-lived objects are moved to an old area that is collected rarely.

question: In the Serial and Parallel collectors, which areas make up the young generation?
options: Eden and two survivor spaces
Eden and the old generation
Metaspace and Eden
Two survivor spaces and the code cache
explanation: The young generation consists of Eden, where new objects are allocated, and two survivor spaces that hold objects which have survived at least one minor collection. The old generation and Metaspace are separate areas.

question: What does a minor collection in the Serial or Parallel collector do with the young generation?
options: Dead objects are freed one by one, and live objects stay in Eden
Every object in Eden is promoted directly to the old generation
The old generation is compacted while the young generation is left untouched
Live objects in Eden and the occupied survivor space are copied out, and those spaces are then reused wholesale
explanation: Young collections are copying collections. Survivors are copied into the empty survivor space (or promoted to the old generation when old enough or when there is no room), and the evacuated spaces are then treated as completely free. Dead objects are never visited individually.

question: Why is a young collection cheap when most young objects are already dead?
options: The collector only has to visit the dead objects
The copying work depends on the amount of live data, not on the amount of dead data
Dead objects are finalized by parallel threads in advance
The young generation is never scanned for roots
explanation: A copying collector touches only the objects it can reach. When almost everything is dead, there is little to copy, so the pause is short even if Eden was full of garbage. Pause time therefore tracks live data, not garbage.

question: What is the maximum value HotSpot accepts for -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold?
explanation: An object's GC age is stored in four bits of its header, so the largest age is 15. Setting the threshold to 15 means survivors can be copied between survivor spaces up to 15 times before promotion, unless the survivor space overflows first.

question: Assume Java 17 on a machine with 4 CPUs and 8 GB of RAM, started with no GC flags. Which collector does HotSpot select by default?
options: Parallel GC
Serial GC
ZGC
G1
explanation: Since Java 9 G1 is the default collector on server-class machines (at least two CPUs and about 1.8 GB of memory). Parallel GC was the default in Java 8. Serial GC is chosen only on machines that do not qualify as server-class.

question: Which JVM option selects the Parallel (throughput) collector?
options: -XX:+UseParallelGC
-XX:+UseThroughputGC
-XX:+UseMultiThreadGC
-XX:ParallelGCThreads=1
explanation: -XX:+UseParallelGC enables the Parallel collector. ParallelGCThreads only sets how many threads a collector uses and does not select a collector. The other two flag names do not exist.

question: Which workload is the best fit for -XX:+UseSerialGC?
options: A multi-terabyte heap with strict pause goals
A throughput batch job running on 64 cores
A small heap in a single-CPU container where low overhead matters
A latency-critical service with a 100 GB heap
explanation: Serial GC uses one thread and stops the application during collection. It has the least bookkeeping and memory overhead, which suits small heaps and single-CPU environments. Large heaps or many cores benefit from the multi-threaded or concurrent collectors.

question: In garbage collection terminology, how do 'concurrent' and 'parallel' differ?
options: Concurrent means several GC threads work while the application is stopped; parallel means GC runs beside the application
Concurrent means one GC thread is used; parallel means many GC threads are used
Concurrent means GC work runs at the same time as application threads; parallel means several GC threads share the work, possibly while the application is stopped
They are synonyms
explanation: Parallel describes how many GC threads split the work. Concurrent describes whether the GC work overlaps with the running application. A collector can be parallel and stop-the-world, as Parallel GC is, or parallel and partly concurrent, as G1 is.

question: Which pair of collectors in Java 17 does all of its collection work while application threads are stopped?
options: G1 and ZGC
Serial and Parallel
Parallel and ZGC
Serial and Shenandoah
explanation: Serial and Parallel are fully stop-the-world, differing in whether one thread or many do the work. G1 runs concurrent marking, and ZGC and Shenandoah do most of their marking and relocation concurrently.

question: Assume Java 17 on Linux. What happens when this command is run?
code: java -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC -version
options: The JVM prints a warning that the option is ignored and starts with its default collector
The JVM starts and uses the CMS collector
The JVM fails with an unrecognized-option error and does not start
The JVM starts with Serial GC and prints no warning
explanation: CMS was deprecated in Java 9 and removed in Java 14. Since then HotSpot recognizes the flag only to print a warning that support was removed, ignores it, and continues with the collector it would normally choose.

question: How does G1 organize the Java heap?
options: Two contiguous areas, young and old, of fixed size
One single region that holds all objects with no generations
One separate heap for each application thread
A set of equal-sized regions that are dynamically assigned roles such as eden, survivor, and old
explanation: G1 divides the heap into many equal-sized regions. A region can serve as eden, survivor, old, or humongous, and the roles change over time. That layout lets G1 collect a chosen subset of regions instead of a whole generation.

question: What range of region sizes (always a power of two) can G1 use?
options: 64 KB to 1 MB
128 KB to 4 MB
1 MB to 8 MB
1 MB to 32 MB
explanation: G1 chooses a region size from 1 MB up to 32 MB, based on the heap size, unless -XX:G1HeapRegionSize overrides it. The value must be a power of two within that range.

question: In G1, an object is called humongous when its size is at least:
options: The size of the whole young generation
One tenth of the maximum heap
Half of a G1 region
Four regions
explanation: Any object of at least 50 percent of the region size is humongous. It is allocated in one or more contiguous regions of its own rather than in eden, which makes allocation of such objects comparatively costly and can cause fragmentation.

question: Which statement about -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 in G1 is correct?
options: It guarantees that no pause will ever exceed 100 ms
It is a soft goal that G1 tries to meet by adjusting generation sizes and the amount of work done per pause
It sets the maximum time allowed between two collections
It applies only to Full GC
explanation: MaxGCPauseMillis expresses a target, not a guarantee. G1 uses its pause-time prediction model to pick how many regions to collect and how large the young generation should be, and it can still exceed the goal. The default target is 200 ms.

question: What does a G1 mixed collection do?
options: It evacuates all young regions plus a selected set of old regions that contain much garbage
It collects only humongous regions
It runs a Full GC together with concurrent marking
It collects only old regions and never young regions
explanation: After concurrent marking has identified how full each old region is, G1 starts a series of mixed collections. Each one evacuates the young regions and some old regions with the most reclaimable space, so old garbage is reclaimed gradually without a full-heap compaction.

question: Which G1 activity runs concurrently with the application threads?
options: Marking live objects across the heap in the concurrent mark phase
The remark pause
Evacuation of young regions during a young pause
Full GC compaction
explanation: Concurrent marking is the part of a G1 cycle that overlaps with the application. Young and mixed evacuation, the remark pause, and Full GC are stop-the-world.

question: Which structure lets a young collection find references from old objects into the young generation without scanning the whole old generation?
options: The string pool
The code cache
The thread stack of the main thread
The card table (and G1's per-region remembered sets), maintained by a write barrier
explanation: Whenever application code stores a reference into a heap object, a write barrier records the card as dirty. A young collection then scans only the dirty cards of old memory as additional roots, instead of the entire old generation.

question: What does SATB mean in G1's concurrent marking?
options: Stop-And-Trace Barrier: all mutator threads pause during marking
Survivor-Age Threshold Balancing: it tunes the tenuring threshold
Snapshot-At-The-Beginning: marking works on the object graph as it was when marking started, and a barrier records overwritten references so they are not missed
Soft-Allocation Tuning Buffer: it sizes thread-local allocation buffers
explanation: With SATB, everything reachable at the start of marking is treated as live. A pre-write barrier saves the old value of a reference field before it is overwritten, so a concurrently running application cannot hide a live object from the marker.

question: Which statement about enabling ZGC in Java 17 is correct?
options: ZGC must be enabled by compiling the application with a special javac flag
-XX:+UseZGC alone is enough, because ZGC stopped being an experimental feature in Java 15
-XX:+UseZGC works only when -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions is also supplied
ZGC is available only on 32-bit JVMs
explanation: ZGC was experimental in Java 11 to 14 and became a product feature in Java 15, so in Java 17 -XX:+UseZGC is sufficient. No compiler option is involved because the choice of collector is a runtime JVM setting.

question: What is the main design goal of ZGC?
options: The highest possible throughput on small heaps
Very short pauses that do not grow with heap size, by doing most work concurrently
The smallest possible memory footprint
Simple single-threaded collection
explanation: ZGC performs marking, relocation, and reference processing concurrently, leaving only very short stop-the-world synchronization points. Its pause times stay low regardless of the live set or heap size, at the cost of some throughput and memory overhead.

question: Which pair of techniques lets ZGC relocate objects while application threads keep running?
options: Colored pointers and load barriers
Card tables and a stop-the-world mark-compact
Reference counting and finalization queues
Tenuring thresholds and survivor spaces
explanation: ZGC stores metadata bits in the reference itself (colored pointers) and runs a load barrier when the application reads a reference from the heap. The barrier detects stale pointers and fixes them, so objects can be moved without stopping the application for the whole move.

question: Which statement about ZGC in Java 17 is correct?
options: It has a young and an old generation, as it did in Java 11
It has a young generation only
It becomes generational when -XX:+ZGenerational is added
It is a single-generation collector in Java 17; generational ZGC arrived in a later release (Java 21)
explanation: In Java 17 ZGC collects the whole heap in each cycle and does not separate young and old objects. The generational mode and its flag were introduced in Java 21, so a Java 17 answer must not assume them.

question: Which statement about Shenandoah in Java 17 is correct?
options: It is the default collector on every build
It is a purely stop-the-world collector
It performs concurrent evacuation for low pauses and is enabled with -XX:+UseShenandoahGC in builds that include it
It was removed in Java 14 together with CMS
explanation: Shenandoah compacts the heap concurrently to keep pauses short. It is a product feature since Java 15 in OpenJDK, but whether it is present depends on the vendor's build, so it is not part of every distribution.

question: What does the Epsilon collector do?
options: It collects only the young generation
It collects only when System.gc() is called
It collects only while the application is idle
It allocates memory but never reclaims it, so the JVM terminates once the heap is exhausted
explanation: Epsilon is a no-op collector meant for performance testing, very short-lived programs, and measuring the overhead of other collectors. Memory is never freed, so an application that allocates more than the heap size fails with OutOfMemoryError.

question: Assume Java 17 on Linux and that app.jar exists. What happens when this command is run?
code: java -XX:+UseEpsilonGC -jar app.jar
options: The JVM starts and uses the Epsilon collector
The JVM refuses to start and reports that the option is experimental and must be unlocked
The JVM ignores the flag and uses G1
The JVM prints a warning and uses Serial GC
explanation: Epsilon is an experimental option in Java 17, so it needs -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions before -XX:+UseEpsilonGC. Without the unlock flag the JVM exits with an error instead of starting.

question: Assume Java 17 on Linux and that app.jar exists. What happens when this command is run?
code: java -XX:+UseSerialGC -XX:+UseParallelGC -jar app.jar
options: The JVM reports conflicting collector combinations and does not start
The last flag wins, so Parallel GC is used
The first flag wins, so Serial GC is used
Serial GC collects the young generation and Parallel GC the old generation
explanation: HotSpot allows only one collector selection. Specifying two different collectors produces a 'Conflicting collector combinations in option list' error and the JVM exits. Flags are not resolved by position.

question: What does -XX:SurvivorRatio=8 mean for the Serial and Parallel collectors?
options: Each survivor space is eight times larger than Eden
The old generation is eight times larger than the young generation
Eden is eight times the size of one survivor space
The JVM uses eight survivor spaces
explanation: SurvivorRatio is the ratio of Eden to one survivor space. With a value of 8 the young generation is split into 8 + 1 + 1 parts, so each survivor space is one tenth of the young generation.

question: With -XX:NewRatio=2 on the Serial or Parallel collector, what fraction of the heap is the young generation?
options: One half
One quarter
One third
Two thirds
explanation: NewRatio is the ratio of the old generation to the young generation. A value of 2 gives old:young = 2:1, so the young generation is one third of the heap and the old generation two thirds.

question: Which option completes the command so the JVM uses a fixed 256 MB young generation?
code: java ____ -jar app.jar
options: -Xmn256m
-Xms256m
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m
-Xss256m
explanation: -Xmn sets both the initial and the maximum size of the young generation. -Xms sets the initial total heap size, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize limits class metadata, and -Xss sets the thread stack size.

question: The survivor spaces are too small to hold the live data of each minor collection. What is the likely consequence?
options: Fewer minor collections occur
Objects overflow into the old generation prematurely, so it fills with objects that would soon have died
Metaspace grows until it reaches its limit
Eden is doubled automatically and nothing else changes
explanation: When survivors do not fit, the excess is promoted regardless of age. This premature promotion raises old-generation occupancy and leads to more frequent, more expensive old-generation collections.

question: What is a TLAB in HotSpot?
options: A table that lists every live object
Reserved Metaspace for each thread's classes
A region in which only threads of equal priority allocate
A chunk of Eden private to one thread, so allocation is a pointer bump without locking
explanation: A thread-local allocation buffer gives each thread its own slice of Eden. Most allocations then only advance a pointer inside that slice, which is fast and needs no synchronization. A new TLAB is requested when the current one is full.

question: Which statement about a Full GC in G1 on Java 17 is correct?
options: It is a stop-the-world collection that compacts the heap, and it uses multiple threads (since Java 10)
It is fully concurrent and causes no pause
It is single-threaded in Java 17
It collects only humongous regions
explanation: G1 falls back to a Full GC when concurrent work cannot keep up. Java 10 made it parallel (JEP 307), but it still stops all application threads and can be long, so frequent Full GCs signal a tuning or sizing problem.

question: What does an evacuation failure (to-space exhausted) mean in G1?
options: Metaspace is full
A thread stack overflowed during collection
G1 found no free regions to copy live objects into during evacuation
A humongous allocation succeeded
explanation: During a pause G1 copies live objects into free regions. If none are left, the evacuation fails, the pause becomes long, and G1 typically follows it with a Full GC. Larger headroom, an earlier marking start, or a bigger heap usually fixes it.

question: In this simplified model an object is promoted once its age reaches the tenuring threshold, and each minor GC it survives increases its age by 1. What is the output?
explanation: Each pass of the loop models one survived minor GC. The age goes 1, 2, 3 and the loop stops when it reaches the threshold of 3, so three minor collections were counted.

question: Pseudocode convention: Eden holds 4 objects. Allocating when Eden is full first triggers a minor GC that empties Eden, because every object is dead. What is printed?
code:
capacity = 4
used = 0
gcCount = 0
for i from 1 to 10:
    if used == capacity then
        gcCount = gcCount + 1
        used = 0
    end if
    used = used + 1
end for
print gcCount
explanation: Allocations 1 to 4 fill Eden. The fifth allocation finds it full and triggers the first GC, and the ninth allocation triggers the second. The tenth allocation fits, so gcCount is 2.

question: Assume Java 17 and formulas that match HotSpot's NewRatio and SurvivorRatio for Serial and Parallel. What is the output?
explanation: With NewRatio 2 the young generation is 300 / 3 = 100 MB. With SurvivorRatio 8 it splits into 10 parts, so each survivor space is 10 MB and Eden is 100 - 20 = 80 MB.

question: Which method completes the code so it sums the number of collections performed by all collectors?
options: getCollectionTime
getMemoryPoolNames
getObjectName
getCollectionCount
explanation: GarbageCollectorMXBean.getCollectionCount() returns how many collections that collector has run. getCollectionTime returns the accumulated time in milliseconds, which is a different quantity.

question: Assume Java 17 running with -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=1m. Which array is allocated as a humongous object?
options: The array a, with 400,000 bytes
The array c, with 100,000 bytes
The array b, with 600,000 bytes
None, because arrays are never humongous
explanation: A 1 MB region is 1,048,576 bytes, so the humongous threshold is 524,288 bytes. Only the 600,000-byte array reaches it. The other two arrays are below half a region and are allocated normally in Eden.

question: A nightly batch job runs on 16 cores and cares only about total completion time, not about individual pauses. Which collector is the best fit?
options: Parallel GC
ZGC
Shenandoah
Serial GC
explanation: Parallel GC uses many threads for stop-the-world collections and has the lowest barrier and bookkeeping overhead, which maximizes throughput. Concurrent collectors trade throughput for shorter pauses, which this job does not need, and Serial GC would leave cores idle.

question: A latency-sensitive service with a 64 GB heap must keep pauses in the low milliseconds. Which Java 17 choice fits best?
options: Serial GC
Parallel GC
ZGC
Epsilon GC
explanation: ZGC is designed for pauses that stay very short even with large heaps. Serial and Parallel pause for the whole collection, which grows with live data, and Epsilon never reclaims memory, so it cannot run a long-lived service.

question: Which statement about a minor collection is correct?
options: It always collects the old generation too
It collects the young generation and treats references from old objects into young objects as roots
It runs only when System.gc() is called
It is always concurrent in G1
explanation: A minor collection looks only at the young generation. A young object referenced only from an old object must still survive, so old-to-young references recorded in the card table or remembered sets act as extra roots. In G1 young pauses are stop-the-world.

question: Does enlarging the young generation always shorten GC pauses?
options: Not necessarily: collections become less frequent, but a pause depends on live data, and a smaller old generation may force more old collections
Yes, always, because pause time is proportional to how often collections occur
Yes, because dead objects are expensive to copy
No, because the young generation size never affects GC behavior
explanation: A bigger young generation lowers collection frequency and gives objects more time to die, but each pause is driven by the live data that must be copied. With a fixed heap it also shrinks the old generation, which can increase the frequency of costly old collections.

question: Which statement about the work done by ZGC in Java 17 is correct?
options: Only marking is concurrent; relocation is stop-the-world
Only relocation is concurrent; marking is stop-the-world
Neither is concurrent; all phases stop the world
Marking and relocation run concurrently, with only brief stop-the-world pauses at phase boundaries
explanation: ZGC stops application threads only for very short synchronization points, such as starting and ending marking and starting relocation. The expensive phases of marking and relocating objects overlap with the application.

question: What is the role of ZGC's load barrier?
options: It stops all threads from reading references while a collection runs
It blocks every read of a primitive field
It zeroes memory the first time it is read
It checks the color of a reference when the application loads it and repairs it if it is stale
explanation: Each time application code loads a reference from the heap, a small piece of code checks the pointer's color bits. If the pointer refers to an old location, the barrier remaps or relocates it, so the thread never works with an outdated address.

question: Which description of G1's collection cycle is correct?
options: Young-only collections run until heap occupancy reaches a threshold, concurrent marking follows, and then mixed collections reclaim old regions until little reclaimable space is left
Mixed collections run first, and young collections start only after the old generation is empty
A Full GC runs first, followed by young collections
Concurrent marking runs after every single young collection
explanation: G1 alternates between a young-only phase and a space-reclamation phase. Marking is started when occupancy passes the initiating threshold, and the mixed collections that follow clean old regions with the most garbage until it is no longer worthwhile.

question: What does -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent control in G1 on Java 17?
options: The percentage of Eden that triggers a minor collection
The heap occupancy at which a concurrent marking cycle starts; its default is 45 percent and G1 adapts it
The share of time the JVM may spend in GC
The size threshold for humongous objects
explanation: G1 starts concurrent marking when overall heap occupancy passes this threshold. Since Java 9 adaptive IHOP is on by default, so the configured value serves as the starting point and G1 adjusts it from observed behavior.

question: How can G1 reclaim old regions without compacting the whole heap?
options: It sweeps dead objects in place and keeps free lists
It relies on reference counts to free objects immediately
It copies live objects out of selected regions into free regions, so the source regions become entirely free
It frees regions by running finalizers
explanation: G1 evacuates live objects from chosen regions into empty regions. This both frees the source regions as a unit and compacts the data it moved, so the heap does not fragment the way an in-place sweep would.

question: Which flag sets the number of threads that G1 uses for its concurrent phases such as marking?
options: -XX:ParallelGCThreads
-XX:ConcGCThreads
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize
explanation: ConcGCThreads controls the threads used while the application runs, such as concurrent marking. ParallelGCThreads controls the threads used inside stop-the-world pauses, so the two settings tune different phases.

question: The array in handle() is needed only during one call. What problem does this code cause in a long-running service that calls handle() repeatedly?
options: Compilation fails because a byte array cannot be stored in a static field
The array is freed at the end of handle(), so the list holds null entries
The static list keeps every array strongly reachable, so the arrays survive minor collections, are promoted, and gradually fill the old generation
The arrays are created in Metaspace, which cannot be collected
explanation: HISTORY is reachable from a class root, and every array added to it stays reachable. Short-lived data therefore behaves like long-lived data and is promoted, which defeats the generational design. The fix is to avoid retaining per-request objects or to bound the collection.

question: Which statement best summarizes the idea behind generational collection?
options: Old objects are scanned on every minor collection, so none can ever die
All objects are promoted after one survival so the old generation is collected first
Objects are grouped by size, and the largest group is collected first
Collect the small young area often and cheaply, and the old area rarely, because most objects die young
explanation: Separating objects by age lets the collector spend frequent, short pauses on the area that holds most garbage. Long-lived objects are moved out of the way and examined much less often.

question: With default G1 settings on Java 17, what does an explicit System.gc() call typically cause?
options: A stop-the-world Full GC, unless flags such as -XX:+DisableExplicitGC or -XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent change that
Nothing, because G1 always ignores it
Only a concurrent mark
Only a young collection
explanation: By default HotSpot treats System.gc() as a request for a full collection, which for G1 is a stop-the-world Full GC. DisableExplicitGC turns the call into a no-op, and ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent makes G1 run a concurrent cycle instead.

question: Pseudocode convention: every object sits on its own card. The write barrier marks the holder's card dirty only when the holder is an old object and the new value is a young object. A dirty card stays dirty until a collection cleans it, and none occurs here. How many cards are dirty after the last statement?
code:
old1 = new OldObject()
old2 = new OldObject()
young1 = new YoungObject()
young2 = new YoungObject()
old1.ref = young1
old2.ref = old1
old1.ref = null
young2.ref = old2
explanation: Only the first store qualifies, because an old holder receives a young value, so old1's card becomes dirty. The second store has an old value, the third stores null, and the fourth has a young holder. Overwriting the reference with null does not clean the card.

question: In the Serial and Parallel collectors, what is a promotion failure?
options: A thread stack overflow during a collection
A failure to load a class while an object is promoted
An OutOfMemoryError thrown immediately by the first minor collection
A minor collection cannot place survivors in the survivor or old space for lack of room, so the JVM falls back to a full collection
explanation: Survivors must be copied somewhere. When neither the survivor space nor the old generation can take them, the minor collection cannot finish normally and a full collection is needed. OutOfMemoryError follows only if that cannot free enough space.

question: Which option completes the command to run G1 with a pause-time goal of 50 ms?
code: java ____ -Xmx4g -jar app.jar
options: -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MinGCPauseMillis=50
-XX:+UseG1GC -XX:GCPauseIntervalMillis=50
-XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=50
-XX:+UseParallelGC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=50
explanation: MaxGCPauseMillis is the flag that sets G1's pause-time goal. MinGCPauseMillis does not exist, GCPauseIntervalMillis sets the desired spacing between pauses rather than their length, and the last choice selects Parallel GC instead of G1.

question: Compared with Parallel GC, which trade-off is typical for G1?
options: Higher throughput and longer pauses
More predictable pauses on large heaps, at the cost of some throughput and extra bookkeeping memory
No pauses at all
Lower memory overhead than every other collector
explanation: G1 spends effort on barriers, remembered sets, and concurrent marking so it can meet a pause goal on big heaps. That extra work lowers peak throughput compared with Parallel GC and costs additional memory.

question: Why is fixing the young generation size with -Xmn generally discouraged when using G1?
options: G1 has no young generation
The flag makes G1 fall back to Serial GC
It removes G1's ability to resize the young generation to meet its pause-time goal
The flag is rejected as a syntax error
explanation: G1 normally adjusts the number of young regions to hit its pause target. A fixed young size overrides that adaptation, so G1 can no longer trade young size against pause time.

question: How does G1 choose the old regions for mixed collections?
options: It prefers regions with the most garbage and skips regions that are too full of live data
It chooses regions strictly by how long ago they were allocated
It chooses regions at random
It chooses only humongous regions
explanation: Concurrent marking records how much live data each old region holds. G1 collects regions with the lowest live ratio first, because evacuating them frees the most space for the least copying, and excludes regions above a liveness threshold (default 85 percent).

question: What is a common reason to set -Xms equal to -Xmx on a long-running server?
options: It disables the young generation
It avoids the work and pauses associated with growing and shrinking the heap
It forces the JVM to use ZGC
It makes finalizers run sooner
explanation: A heap that starts at its maximum size does not need to be resized as load changes, which removes one source of variability. The trade-off is that the full amount of memory is reserved from the start.

question: In G1, what is the typical consequence when allocation outpaces concurrent marking and space reclamation until no free regions remain?
options: G1 throws OutOfMemoryError immediately without trying anything else
G1 switches to the CMS collector
Young collections stop and old collections take over
G1 performs a stop-the-world Full GC, causing a long pause, and an OutOfMemoryError follows only if that cannot free enough space
explanation: The concurrent and incremental work is meant to keep up with allocation. When it cannot, G1 falls back to a Full GC that stops the application and compacts the heap. Frequent occurrences call for a larger heap, an earlier marking threshold, or less promotion.

question: Which option enables basic garbage collection logging (one line per collection) through the unified logging framework in Java 17?
options: -Xgc:info
-XX:GCLog=info
-Xlog:gc
-verbose:heap
explanation: Since Java 9 (JEP 158) all JVM logging goes through -Xlog. The gc tag at the default info level prints one summary line per collection. The other flag names do not exist.

question: If no -Xlog option is supplied, what does a Java 17 JVM log by default?
options: Warnings and errors from all log tags, written to stdout
Every gc event at info level, written to stdout
Nothing at all
Only pause events, written to a file named gc.log
explanation: The default configuration is equivalent to all tags at warning level going to stdout. GC pause lines at info level are not printed unless -Xlog:gc (or similar) is added. No log file is created unless one is requested.

question: Assume Java 17 on Linux. Which command writes GC logs to the file gc.log and adds the wall-clock time decorator?
options: java -Xlog:gc=gc.log:time -jar app.jar
java -Xlog:gc:time:file=gc.log -jar app.jar
java -Xlog:file=gc.log:gc:time -jar app.jar
java -Xlog:gc:file=gc.log:time -jar app.jar
explanation: The -Xlog syntax is selectors, then output, then decorators, then output options, separated by colons. So the tag comes first, then file=gc.log, then time. The other forms put the fields in the wrong order or use the level position for a file name.

question: What does 24M->3M(256M) mean in this log line?
code: [1.234s][info][gc] GC(7) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 24M->3M(256M) 3.456ms
options: The heap held 3M before and 24M after the pause, with 256M as the maximum
Heap occupancy was 24M before the collection and 3M after it, and the heap currently has 256M committed
24M is the young generation, 3M the old generation, and 256M the Metaspace
24M was freed, 3M is still in use, and 256M is reserved for the next collection
explanation: The first number is heap occupancy before the pause, the second is occupancy after it, and the value in parentheses is the current heap capacity (committed size). Reading the arrow as before to after is the key rule.

question: By how many megabytes did heap occupancy drop in this collection?
code: [2.500s][info][gc] GC(3) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 120M->20M(512M) 8.5ms
explanation: Occupancy went from 120M to 20M, a drop of 100M. The 20M remaining are survivors and promoted objects that are still live, and the 512M in parentheses is capacity, not usage.

question: Which statement best summarizes pause time and throughput?
options: Pause time is the total time spent in GC, and throughput is the longest single pause
Pause time is how often collections happen, and throughput is how long each one lasts
They measure the same thing in different units
Pause time is how long application threads are stopped in one event, and throughput is the share of total time spent running application code rather than GC
explanation: A pause is one stop-the-world interval, so its length matters for latency. Throughput is the fraction of overall time not spent on GC, which matters for batch work. Tuning for one often costs the other.

question: Pseudocode convention: / is real division and * is multiplication. What is printed?
code:
totalSeconds = 200
pauseSeconds = 5 + 3
throughputPercent = (totalSeconds - pauseSeconds) * 100 / totalSeconds
print throughputPercent
explanation: GC time is 8 seconds out of 200, so application time is 192 seconds. 192 * 100 / 200 is 96 percent throughput.

question: In the log of a Serial or Parallel collector, what does the cause Pause Young (Allocation Failure) indicate?
options: A young collection was triggered because Eden could not satisfy an allocation request; this is normal and not an error
The JVM threw an OutOfMemoryError for the allocating thread
The operating system refused to give the JVM native memory
A bug in the collector forced a restart of the JVM
explanation: Allocation Failure is the ordinary trigger for a young collection: the allocation did not fit, so the JVM collected and retried. It does not mean allocation ultimately failed.

question: In a Java 17 G1 log, which entry marks the young pause in which a concurrent marking cycle is started?
options: Pause Young (Concurrent Start)
Pause Young (Normal)
Pause Full (System.gc())
Pause Cleanup
explanation: G1 piggybacks the start of concurrent marking on a young pause, which the log labels Concurrent Start. A Normal young pause does not begin marking, and Cleanup is a later stop-the-world step of the cycle.

question: Within a G1 concurrent marking cycle, which pair of log entries are stop-the-world pauses?
options: Concurrent Mark and Concurrent Rebuild Remembered Sets
Concurrent Mark and Pause Remark
Pause Remark and Pause Cleanup
Concurrent Clear Claimed Marks and Pause Cleanup
explanation: Remark and Cleanup stop the application, while entries named Concurrent run alongside it. Only those two pauses of the cycle (apart from the initial young pause) count toward stopped time.

question: What does the cause in this log line tell you?
code: [310.200s][info][gc] GC(41) Pause Full (System.gc()) 800M->300M(1024M) 950.000ms
options: The heap was exhausted by a memory leak
Code in the application or a library called System.gc() (or an equivalent request), and -XX:+DisableExplicitGC would suppress it
Metaspace reached its threshold
A humongous allocation failed
explanation: The text in parentheses names the cause. System.gc() means an explicit request triggered the Full GC. The JVM did not run out of space by itself, so the fix is to find and remove the caller or disable explicit collections.

question: Assume Java 17. Which command keeps five GC log files of at most 10 MB each?
options: java -Xlog:gc:file=gc.log:time:logrotate=5x10M -jar app.jar
java -Xlog:gc:file=gc.log:filecount=5,filesize=10M:time -jar app.jar
java -Xlog:gc:file=gc.log:time,filecount=5,filesize=10M -jar app.jar
java -Xlog:gc:file=gc.log:time:filecount=5,filesize=10M -jar app.jar
explanation: File rotation options go in the last colon-separated field, after the decorators. Putting them before the decorators or inside the decorator list makes them invalid, and logrotate is not an option name.

question: How do -Xlog:gc and -Xlog:gc* differ?
options: -Xlog:gc* prints only pause lines, while -Xlog:gc prints every GC-related tag
They are identical
-Xlog:gc* selects all tags and -Xlog:gc selects none
-Xlog:gc selects only the tag set exactly named gc, while -Xlog:gc* also selects tag sets that include gc together with other tags, such as gc+heap or gc+cpu
explanation: Without the wildcard the selector matches only the exact tag combination. The trailing asterisk widens it to every tag set that begins with or contains those tags, producing much more detail.

question: Which unified-logging decorator prints the time elapsed since the JVM started?
options: time
uptime
pid
tid
explanation: uptime shows seconds since JVM start, and it is part of the default decorators. time prints the wall-clock date and time instead, and pid and tid identify the process and thread.

question: Which command lists the available log tags, levels, and decorators in Java 17?
options: java -Xlog:help
java -XX:+PrintLogTags
java -Xlog:list
java -help:gc
explanation: -Xlog:help prints the supported syntax, tags, levels, and decorators. The other forms are not valid JVM options.

question: What does -Xlog:gc+age=trace add to GC logging?
options: The CPU time of each pause
The list of classes loaded into Metaspace
The age distribution of survivors, showing how much data of each age survived the collection
Stack traces of the GC worker threads
explanation: The gc+age tag at trace level prints a table of survivor ages. It helps judge whether the tenuring threshold and survivor sizes suit the application, for example to detect premature promotion.

question: What is the output?
explanation: The pattern needs digits followed by M->, so GC(12) does not match. The match is 64M->8M(256M), giving before 64 and after 8, and the program prints their difference, 56.

question: What is the output?
explanation: The arguments are init, used, committed, and max. The expression is used * 100 / max, which is 300 * 100 / 1000 = 30, followed by the percent sign. Using committed instead of max is the common mistake.

question: An application allocates 300 MB per second and has a 600 MB Eden. Assume Eden fills completely before each young collection and the collection itself takes negligible time. How often does a young collection occur?
options: every 0.5 seconds
every 1 second
every 1.5 seconds
every 2 seconds
explanation: The interval between young collections is Eden size divided by allocation rate: 600 MB / 300 MB per second = 2 seconds. A faster allocation rate or a smaller Eden shortens the interval.

question: What best explains User being much larger than Real in this line?
code: [5.000s][info][gc,cpu] GC(3) User=0.40s Sys=0.02s Real=0.05s
options: The system clock is inaccurate
Several GC worker threads ran in parallel, so CPU time summed over all threads exceeds elapsed wall time
Application threads kept running during the pause
The pause was caused by swapping
explanation: User and Sys add up CPU time across all threads, while Real is elapsed wall-clock time. With about eight workers busy for 0.05 seconds, the CPU total can reach 0.4 seconds.

question: Which cause is most plausible for this pause?
code: [9.000s][info][gc,cpu] GC(5) User=0.02s Sys=0.01s Real=0.90s
options: Too many parallel GC threads were used
The GC threads spent most of the pause waiting, for example on disk I/O or swapping, or without CPU because of contention
A concurrent marking phase ran during the pause
A humongous allocation took place
explanation: Real time far above User plus Sys means the threads were mostly not running on a CPU. Typical reasons are swapped-out heap pages, slow storage, or CPU starvation, not GC algorithm work.

question: Which option logs how long application threads were stopped at safepoints for any reason, not only for GC?
options: -Xlog:gc+heap
-Xlog:gc+cpu
-Xlog:safepoint
-Xlog:class+load
explanation: The safepoint tag reports each safepoint operation with its reason and timings. A GC pause is only one kind of safepoint, so gc logs alone can miss other stop events.

question: What is time-to-safepoint?
options: The delay while the JVM waits for every application thread to reach a safepoint; it adds to the stopped time before GC work begins
The time GC worker threads spend copying survivors
The interval between two consecutive young collections
The time spent in concurrent marking
explanation: Before a stop-the-world operation can start, every Java thread must reach a safepoint. A thread that is slow to arrive keeps all the others waiting, so the visible freeze is longer than the GC work itself.

question: Every GC pause in a service's log is under 20 ms, yet users sometimes see freezes of about 300 ms. Which explanation is plausible and invisible in the pause lines?
options: Concurrent marking runs on the application threads
Young collections run concurrently with the application
The heap is too large
Slow arrival at the safepoint or non-GC safepoint operations stopped threads outside the intervals that the GC pause lines measure
explanation: The pause lines time the collection work, not the time spent waiting for threads to reach the safepoint or other safepoint operations. Safepoint logging reveals those stops.

question: In Java 17, which log entries are the stop-the-world pauses of a ZGC cycle?
options: Concurrent Mark, Concurrent Mark Free, and Concurrent Relocate
Pause Mark Start, Concurrent Mark, and Concurrent Relocate
Pause Mark Start, Pause Mark End, and Concurrent Relocate
Pause Mark Start, Pause Mark End, and Pause Relocate Start
explanation: ZGC has three short pauses: the start of marking, the end of marking, and the start of relocation. Everything labeled Concurrent runs alongside the application.

question: What does an Allocation Stall entry in a ZGC log mean?
options: A thread had to wait for memory because allocation outpaced the concurrent collection; more heap or more concurrent GC threads usually helps
A thread was waiting to reach a safepoint
Metaspace has been exhausted
A Full GC is running
explanation: ZGC reclaims memory concurrently. If the application allocates faster than the collector frees, allocating threads are stalled until memory is available. That is a sizing problem, not a normal pause.

question: Which GC cause in a log means that growth of class metadata triggered the collection?
options: Allocation Failure
Ergonomics
Metadata GC Threshold
G1 Humongous Allocation
explanation: Metadata GC Threshold appears when Metaspace usage crosses its high-water mark, so the JVM collects in order to unload classes and adjust the threshold. Frequent occurrences point to class-loading churn or an undersized initial Metaspace.

question: A G1 log repeatedly shows Pause Young (Concurrent Start) (G1 Humongous Allocation). What does it suggest?
options: The old generation is empty
Objects of at least half a region are being allocated and trigger concurrent cycles; a larger region size or avoiding giant arrays may help
Application code calls System.gc()
The JVM is using ZGC
explanation: The cause names the trigger. Humongous allocations go straight to old space and can push occupancy past the marking threshold, so frequent cycles started this way point to large object allocation.

question: Assume a JVM with PID 4321 on Linux. Which command asks the JVM to run a garbage collection from outside the process, equivalent to calling System.gc()?
options: jcmd 4321 GC.run
jcmd 4321 GC.heap_info
jstat -gcutil 4321
jinfo -flag +UseG1GC 4321
explanation: The diagnostic command GC.run triggers a collection like System.gc(). GC.heap_info only prints heap details, jstat only reports statistics, and jinfo cannot change the collector of a running JVM.

question: In jstat -gcutil output, what does the YGCT column show?
options: The number of young collections so far
The number of full collections so far
The total time spent in all collections, in seconds
The total time spent in young collections, in seconds
explanation: YGC is the count of young collections and YGCT is their accumulated time. FGC and FGCT are the same for full collections, and GCT is the total GC time.

question: Assume a JVM with PID 4321 on Linux. What does this command do?
code: jstat -gcutil 4321 1000 5
options: Prints one sample and then waits 1000 seconds
Samples every 5 milliseconds, 1000 times
Samples GC utilization every 1000 milliseconds, five times, and then exits
